sentences.text: The application was allowed and counterpart was directed to be sent to the CFL for analysis.
The sample was examined by the Director CFL and he gave his certificate dated 09.07.2001 opining the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained vegetable oil.
5. Thereafter matter was listed for pre-charge evidence, wherein the complainant examined PW-1 Sh. Jeet Ram, Food Inspector.

6. On the basis of testimony of PW-1 on 04.08.2008 charge was framed against the appellants/accused for commission of offences punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act for violation of provisions of Section 2(ia)(a),(j) and (m) of PFA Act alleging therein that on 30.08.2000 at about 05.00 p.m, the appellant being the the Vendor cum Proprietor of M/s Balaji Sweet Corner, 128 Railway Road, Shahdara, Delhi-32 was found vending various food article including Burfee and sold its sample of about 1500 grams for analysis bearing no label or declaration ready for sale, taken from an open tray to Food Inspector on payment of sample commodity in the presence of LHA and witnesses and it was analyzed by Public Analyst vide Certificate No. G14-4/2001-230 dated 09.07.2007 and it was found that the sample is adulterated because added colour i.e. 2.2ppm tartrazine present, vegetable oil present and thereby violated the provisions of Section 2(ia)(a)(j)
and (m) of PFA Act, and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 16(1)(a) of CA no.
56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA PFA Act, 1954 read with Section 7 of the PFA Act to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
6.1

During trial after the examination and detailed cross examination of witnesses of the department i.e. PW1 Sh. Jeet Ram, Food Inspector, PW2 Ms. Suniti Kumar Gupta and PW3 Sh.Satnam Singh,
Secretary, APMC,GMNCT of Delhi the then SDM/LHA, prosecution evidence was closed and matter was fixed for Statement of accused.

7. The statement of appellant/accused was recorded under section 313 Cr.PC in which he pleaded his innocence and stated that no efforts were made by the Food Inspector to join public witnesses no price was paid by the Food Inspector, sample was not sent in his presence, the tray was pasted by vegetable oil to avoid sticking of Burfee with the tray ; complaint was filed a routine manner, CFL report is wrong he did not apply his proper method of analyzing the sample, it is a false case ; he was not selling any food item having khoya as ingredient ; under the pressure and duress he made endorsement on Ex PW1/B The burfee was made from left out items such as besan, maida sugar and khaand and he preferred to lead defence evidence but despite opportunities no defence witness was examined.

7.1 After hearing the arguments of both the parties, appellant was convicted by the learned trial court for commission of offence punishable under section punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act for violation of Section 2(ia) and (a) of PFA Act, 1954 Mukut Lal vs The State ( Govt Of Nct Of Delhi ) on 15 January, 2021 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/25081329/

The State / DA 28.02.2017 observed that the samples had been collected according to the prescribed procedures from the premises of vendor cum Proprietor/appellant, on analyzing the sample, it was opined vide PA report that the food sample is adulterated, appellant had sold adulterated food in violation of Section 2(ia)(a) and (m) of PFA Act and has committed the offence punishable u/s 7/16(1)(a) PFA Act.

sentences.text: The appellant was accordingly convicted and sentenced by the learned trial court and aggrieved by the said judgment and order on quantum of sentence dated 01.03.2017, the present appeal has been preferred by the appellant.
9.(I) The appellant has assailed the judgment and order on sentence passed by the learned trial court by urging various grounds.

II) Alternatively, on the quantum of sentence, relying upon the new legislation, it was pleaded that the case of the appellant be considered sympathetically in the light of the preposition of law laid down by the Hon'ble Courts pursuant to coming of new legislation that is Food Safety & Standards Act.

10. During the course of argument on 06.01.2021, learned counsel for the appellant submitted that appellant is not challenging the merits of the case/ conviction decided by the learned trial court vide judgment dated 28.02.2017 and is confining his appeal limited to the quantum of sentence only,
awarded to him vide order dated 01.03.2017 ; and to confirm his submissions appellant has tender his statement in this regard and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him by giving him the benefit of New Legislation as FSSAI.
CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs.
Vs. The State / DA 11.

Learned counsel for the Delhi Admn./Food Department, objected to the same and submitted that according to statement of appellant, prosecution has established its case and he be sentenced with strict punishment in terms of old Act wherein minimum punishment is prescribed and no leniency should be shown to the convict as it is a serious offence of food adulteration article / commodity leading to hazardous consequences on the health or body of a person.
12. I have carefully gone through the available record as well as trial court record, have heard the submissions of learned counsel for both the parties at length and have also gone through the judgments relied upon by the parties.
13.

In light of above submissions and discussion particularly when the statement of appellant is recorded, I find no valid and legal reasons to interfere with the well reasoned judgment of the learned trial court.
The findings of the learned trial court with respect to the conviction of the appellant for the offence punishable under 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act read with Section 7 of the PFA Act, 1954 are upheld.
II. Now Coming to the alternate plea of giving benefit of new legislation to the appellant/ accused.

sentences.text: It is argued by learned counsel for the appellant that on the date of pronouncement of judgment/order on sentence, the PFA Act, 1954 was repealed and new act had come into operation.

It is stated that the court should give benefit of the new legislation to the accused vide which the punishment provided under the old act has been diluted to a considerable extent, and that the offence for which CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA the accused/appellant has been convicted now falls under the category of "Unsafe Food" punishable under section 59 of the new Act i.e Food and Safety Standards Act, 2006 (hereinafter called FSSAI) punishable only with fine upto Rs. Five lacs.
15.

entities.text: CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
It was argued by learned counsel for the appellant that appellant is respectable person of society,
has deep roots in the society, has responsibility towards his family, not involved in any other case,
suffering from some diseases, has no other source of income except vegetable selling and prayed that a lenient view be taken against him in the light of the provisions of law under the new Act.

15.1 Further that case pertains to the year 2006, the appellant/accused has faced the trial almost 14 years which by itself is a sufficient punishment and the hardships faced by him has caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him.

15.2 In support of his submissions, learned counsel for appellant had relied upon the judgment of Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016, vide order dated 10.03.2016, as corrected vide order dated 17.03.2016, as reported in 2016 (1) FAC 203 ) of Hon'ble Supreme Court and earlier judgment T Barai Vs. Henry 1983 ( ) SCC 177. 15.3 Per contra, learned SPP, strongly opposed the submissions CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA advanced by learned counsel by addressing that the sentencing cannot be done in new Act since the definition of many offences are changed in the new Act including this particular offence of which accused is charged.

entities.text: Nemi Chand Vs. State of Rajasthan ( Crl. Appeals No. 214 and 215 of 2016
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Definition of major offences like "adulteration" and "misbranding" have been changed.

Now FSSAI have definition "substandard food", "food containing extraneous matter" "unsafe food"
and misbranded food".
Due to this reason, the ingredients have changed and thus there is no way in which the old offences could be related to new offences.
15.4 As far as the objection of learned SPP is concerned, in the present case, the offence was that the article/food was found adulterated and was unfit for human consumption.

This was violation of Rules under PFA Rules and thus termed as adulteration in view of Section 2(1a)(a) & (m) of the PFA Act and thus consequently punishable under section 16(1A) of PFA Act read with Section 7 of PFA Act.
15.5
That now in the FSSAI such adulteration is definedand fall under "Substandard food" in terms of Section 3(zx) of FSSAI Act and violation thereof is punishable u/s 51 of FSSA.
So if we go through both these provisions of law a particular offence with a particular fact is mentioned with some other name but with same ingredients in the New FSSA Act.

sentences.text: Further, the charge in this case was framed for the said offences and there is no charge in which it is stated that the sample commodity was injuries to health.
Had it been the case, the charge should have been for the offence punishable u/s 16(1-A)(ii) of PFA CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA Act read with Section 2(ia)(l) and (f).

sentences.text: In fact, there is categorical finding by the learned trial court that appellant is not prosecuted, nor sufficient material on record, to make out the case rendering the food articles injuries to health.
15.7 Thus, it is observed that it is the ingredients which constitute an offence determines whether it is the same offence but with new name or an altogether different offence,
Here the offence committed by the appellant was punishable u/s 16(1)(a) PFA Act is similar to the offence u/s 51 of FSSAI Act, which is now punishable only with fine upto rupees five lakhs.
15.8 Now,coming to the application of Nemi Chand Judgment (supra) is concerned, the same is based on the old judgment i.e. T Barai ( Supra) of Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The relevant portion of the T Barai Judgment is as follows :
- (Para 25) It is settled both on authority and principle that when a later statute again describes an offence created by an earlier statute and imposes a different punishment or varies the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by implication in Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80 Lord Campbell put the matter thus :
- "It is well settled rule of construction that, if a later statute again describes an ofence created by a former statute and affixes a different punishment, varying the procedure, the earlier statute is repealed by the later statute see also Smith Vs.
Benabo ( 1937) 1 ALL ER 523 : ( 1997) 1 KB 518: 156 LT 194"
- In Regina Vs. Youle ( 1861) 158 ER 311,315-16 : LT 299 : 9 CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA WR 637 Martin B. said in the oft-quoted passage :
-

Michell Vs.
Brown ( 1958) 120 ER 909, 912 : 32 LTOS 146:7 WR 80
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If a statute deals with a particular class of offences, and a subsequent Act is passed which deals with precisely the same offence, and a different punishment is imposed by the later Act, I think that, in effect, the legislature has declared that the new Act shall be substituted for the earlier Act."

- The rule is however subject to the limitation contained in Article 20(1) against ex post facto law providing for a greater punishment and has also no application where the offence described in the later Act is not the same as in the earlier Act i.e. when the essential ingredients of the two offences are different.

- Moreover, this particular aspect is stated as a illustration in the same judgment in Para 23 which is as follows :

To illustrate, if Parliament were to reenact Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and provide that the punishment for an offence of murder shall be sentence for imprisonment for life instead of the present sentence of death or imprisonment for life, then it can not be that the courts would still award a sentence of death even in pending cases.
- Academic Reference can also be made to the letter dated 03.10.2017 of Food Safety and Standards Authority of India, produced before the court during the proceedings.

entities.text: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
entities.label: ORG

sentences.text: Vide said letter the said authority, in the light of judgment of Hon'ble Supreme Court in Nemi Chand's Case (supra) issued an advisory to the Commissioners of Food Safety/Officers incharge of Food Safety to dispose of the long pending court cases filed under old PFA Act CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA mainly concerning substandard and misbranding by imposing fine only.
- In view of the above mentioned discussion, it can be safely said that while considering on the point of sentence, the quantum of sentence in new Act i.e. FSSA is to be considered.

16. Thus analyzing the facts of the case, taking note of the special circumstances of the case and the fact that accused is suffering from various medial ailments, is almost bed ridden, hardly able to walk properly, 82 years of age, further matter is pending consideration for the last 21 years ; case pertains to the year 2000 and the applicant has faced rigors of trial for about 20 years or so which by itself is a sufficient punishment and the hardships faced by him caused him great mental agony, stress and rigors of trial during the said period.

It is also stated that now a days special circumstances exists due to outbreak of pandemic of Covid-19 and there are chances of appellant being infected with virus in case imprisonment of sentence is awarded to him and in light of the above cited judgment and the judgment of Hon'ble High Court of Delhi titled as GNCT Vs. Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.

Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 01.09.2017 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of 06 months stands waived of to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court and the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs. 10,000/- to Rs. 15,000/-
In CA no. 56/17 Mukut Lal Vs. Vs. The State / DA default of payment of fine the appellant/convict shall undergo simple imprisonment for two months.

Jagdish Tyagi dated 11.10.2017 in my view the convict/ appellant is entitled to the benefit of new legislation.
Accordingly to meet the ends of justice, the sentence of the convict as imposed by the learned trial court vide order dated 01.09.2017 stands modified to the extent that the order sentencing the appellant to undergo simple imprisonment of 06 months stands waived of to simple imprisonment for one day i.e. till rising of the court and the sentence of fine is enhanced from Rs. 10,000/- to Rs. 15,000/-
